plate_findings.evidence: Caption: 'Hyperpigmentation in her lips, tongue, and mucosal regions'; in-text: 'hyperpigmentation in her lips, tongue, and mucosal regions (Figure 1)'

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Real-patient clinical photograph of the lower face and protruded tongue showing mucosal hyperpigmentation, a textbook manifestation of primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease); caption and in-text explicitly attribute these findings to the patient, and the article title centers on diagnosing Addison's disease. B: Real-patient clinical photograph of both hands showing fingernails with grey-black longitudinal melanonychia, captioned as the patient's nails and confirmed in the in-text; the article title identifies melanonychia with pseudo-Hutchinson sign as an aid to diagnosing Addison's disease. Melanonychia is a recognized but less common manifestation, hence variant; no vocabulary key exists for it, so it is proposed. C: Real-patient clinical photograph of both feet showing toenails with grey-black longitudinal melanonychia, part of the captioned nail findings and described in the in-text in the context of the Addison's disease...

panels.rationale: Single axial contrast CT of the abdomen from a patient with biochemically confirmed primary adrenal insufficiency (low baseline cortisol 13 mg/dL, absent ACTH response, ACTH 217 pg/mL, low urinary free cortisol) in a disease-focused article ("Acute adrenal insufficiency secondary to bilateral adrenal B-cell lymphoma"). The only enlarged-adrenal CT vocabulary entry is the calcified-enlarged key; the clearly supported feature is bilateral adrenal enlargement (calcification is not explicitly stated, hence confidence 0.7 and the precise finding is also listed under proposed_findings). panels.rationale: Single clinical photograph of abdomen with caption explicitly attributing waistband hyperpigmentation to primary adrenal insufficiency/Addison's disease, supported by in-text mention of skin hyperpigmentation supporting clinically probable APS-2. Friction-accentuated hyperpigmentation is a classic manifestation.
panels.attribution_text: Luo et al. Case Report: Primary aldosteronism coexisting with adrenal insufficiency in a 73-year-old woman with paradoxical hyponatremia. Frontiers in immunology None. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Skin hyperpigmentation in the waistband area, attributable to chronic friction, supporting the diagnosis of primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison’s disease).
in_text_mentions: However, plasma ACTH levels sent to an external laboratory showed no circadian variation (08:00 7.19 pmol/L, 16:00 1.21 pmol/L, 00:00 1.68 pmol/L; reference 1.60–13.90 pmol/L), which was discordant with the cortisol rhythm. In addition, pituitary MRI was normal, excluding structural lesions. Given the absence of confirmatory 21-hydroxylase antibody testing and ACTH-stimulation testing, the physical examination finding of skin hyperpigmentation (Figure 2) and her history of Hashimoto's thyroiditis supported only a clinically probable diagnosis of APS-2 (7, 8).

in_text_mentions: Given the nonspecific gastrointestinal and constitutional symptoms alongside hypotension, a possible adrenal crisis was considered. An abdominal computed tomography (CT) scan (Figures 1, 2) revealed bilateral adrenal gland thickening with periadrenal fat stranding, without evidence of hemorrhage, findings suggestive of acute nonhemorrhagic adrenalitis.
